summary: Maryland front range light off North Point, built 1886 on the 1822 North Point pier; electrified 1929 and unmanned since; Coast Guard-owned, reached by boat, closed.

structures.note: 22 ft (6.7 m) tower per NRHP 2002; the nomination also reports 18 ft (1896 Light List), 22 ft (1994 list), 27 ft (de Gast 1993) and 25 ft above water (1885-1886 Board reports)
Former stone foundation of the 1822 North Point Lighthouse; 30-foot square pier (nomination)

staffing.note: Electrified 28 November 1929; unmanned since (NRHP). USLHS records automation in 1914 (see corrections).

access.note: Owned and managed by the Coast Guard; access by boat (NRHP); USLHS: not open to the public

events.note: Congress appropriates $25,000 on 3 March 1885 for range lights at the new cut-off from Craighill Channel
Octagonal brick tower built on the old North Point stone foundation; all work completed by the end of June 1886
Both range beacons first lighted 15 January 1886, before the dwellings were finished
Severe storm of 28 August 1893 carries away the timber-and-stone bridge from the beacon to shore; keeper's quarters on shore abandoned
Beacon fitted for keeper occupancy: lamp moved to an exterior iron platform; boat landing and davits; completed October 1893
Oil house: the nomination says a 55-can iron house was erected; the Board's 1894 report describes a 1,000-gallon sheet-iron house bought for the station. Not reconciled.
USLHS place record gives automation in 1914; conflicts with the 1929 electrification and unmanned status in the nomination and the 1930 Bulletin
Electrified November 1929 from the Fort Howard lighting system by 650-foot submarine cable; unmanned since (NRHP; Bulletin 1930)
One unnamed report says the tower was torn down in the late 1930s and rebuilt in 1938; the nomination thinks the present tower is the original 1886 tower; Turbyville disputes the 1938 date

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Two Craighill Channel front lights exist. The Board's 1900 repair list names 'Craighill Channel, front' (the lower front at Sparrows Point) and 'Cutoff Channel, front' (this station) separately. The lower front roster places that station at Sparrows Point.

corrections.why: The nomination says electricity came on 28 November 1929 and the light has been unmanned since; the 1930 Bulletin dates the electrification to November 1929. The archive's 1914 automation date and its 'Custodian' entries to 1917 are not explained by any source read. Human check of the USLHS entry before any change.

corrections.proposed: fixed red (nomination, 2002); confirm against a current Light List
corrections.why: The nomination and the 1930 Bulletin both describe a red light. The station record gives a white isophase characteristic. The Light List (USCG LLNR 2-8090) was not read; a human check is needed before any change.

notes_for_editor: IDENTITY: Two Craighill Channel front lights exist. This station is the Cut-off (North Point) front, which the USLHS, NRHP and the Board's 1900 repair list keep separate from the Craighill Channel lower front at Sparrows Point. Bulletin and Commissioner entries that say only 'Craighill Channel Range Front' were NOT attributed to this station. The archive's roster for the lower front lists Lloyd V. Gaskill and Jorgen B. Johansen as keepers there, so the 1919-1924 tows and the 1916 collision belong to the lower front or are ambiguous, and are not used. STAFFING: the archive's 'Year Automated: 1914' and 'Custodian' 1914-1917 conflict with the nomination (electricity 1929, unmanned since) and with the 1930 Bulletin; no keeper for this station after 1917 is named in any source read. The archive lists Frederick Burmeister as head keeper 1888-1914 and Frederick W.M. Burmeister as first assistant 1895-1914 at this station, under separate person slugs; check the register images before treating them as two men. CHARACTERISTIC: station record Iso W 6s (ENC) against the nomination's 'fixed red' and the 1930 Bulletin's red light; a current Light List check (USCG LLNR 2-8090) is needed. HEIGHT: the nomination gives 25 ft above water (1885-1886 Board accounts), 15 ft (light elevation, 2002), 22 ft (tower, 2002), 18 ft (1896 Light List), 22 ft (1994 list), 27 ft (de Gast 1993); the record's 5.5 m (about 18 ft) is not checked. The Board's 1894 volume (scan p. 422) reads 'August 28, 1803' in OCR; 1893 is the year in the nomination and the Board's 1894 context, so the story takes the date from the nomination. Check the page image before quoting the year from the Board. OIL HOUSE: the nomination says a 55-can iron oil house was erected at the front in 1894; the Board's 1894 report describes a 1,000-gallon sheet-iron house bought for this beacon; the Board's 1895 report lists a 55-can house at the 'Cutoff Channel range (rear)'. The story states the disagreement and does not resolve it. 1938 REBUILD: the nomination's 'one report' is unnamed; Clifford (1994) and Turbyville (1995) are cited in the nomination only; the nomination's boundary note also says 'the 1938 New Cut-off Front Range tower'. The 1822 North Point light date comes from the nomination only. NEWSPAPERS: a Chronicling America search for 'Cut-off Channel' in Maryland papers, 1885-1930, returned two pages that do not concern the light (Evening Capital, Annapolis, 1887; Prince George's Enquirer, 1899); not used. The 1900 Board listing is a repair list, not a description of the work. NEWSPAPERS (resume run): a Chronicling America search for 'Craighill Channel' with 'light keeper' in Maryland papers, 1886-1917, returned four pages; one (Evening Capital, Annapolis, 12 March 1892) mentions a 'Craighill Channel light at Fair Haven', which is not this station and is not used. No newspaper is used in the story. FACT-CHECK 2026-10-22: the 1900 repair list ('Craighill Channel, front' and 'Cutoff Channel, front', scan p. 117) was read from OCR running text, not the page image. The nomination dates Robert de Gast's book 1993 in its note 2 but 1973 in its bibliography; the story now gives the book without a date. The 1894 oil-house entry and bridge date are read from OCR (the Board's storm date prints as 'August 28, 1803'); the story takes 28 August 1893 from the nomination, which the Board's fiscal year and context support.
